title: A third company linked to suspected money laundering
summary: Bank F’s network tool found phone numbers and email addresses shared by three companies. Further account checks indicated possible money laundering.
account: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's report “AML/CFT Regtech: Case Studies and Insights” (January 2021; press release 21 January 2021) presents anonymized bank case studies. Bank F is a subsidiary and regional head office of a large global bank in Asia-Pacific, per the report. It implemented a network (graph) analytics solution in Hong Kong in 2013. It identified high-risk customers and transactions from wholesale client, correspondent banking, trade, payments and external registry data. In a 2015 example, a relationship manager gathered intelligence about trade-based money laundering (TBML) related to a drug cartel in one account. The manager linked it to a second account via the CRM tool. The tool then identified additional companies linked to the first two parties through linked phone numbers and email addresses. Account reviews for Companies A, B and C revealed potential money laundering concerns. The report states that by 2016 Bank F covered its top 20 commercial banking sites and about 80% of its trade lending book. The tool has led to review of around 100 customer relationships holding around USD 500 million in clean or unsecured exposures, it says. The report’s USD 50 million figure assumes that 10% of those exposures would otherwise be unrecoverable. It does not document USD 50 million in realized savings. The foreword adds that such techniques are already neutralizing mule account networks linked to face mask scams. The 2015 example carries no day.
purpose: Identify high-risk customers, transactions and hidden relationships for AML/CFT and trade-based money laundering investigations.
system: Bank F network (graph) analytics solution implemented in Hong Kong in 2013
developer: Bank F (anonymized subsidiary and regional head office of a large global bank); the report names no vendor
segment: Trade finance and trade-based money laundering

ratings.reason: The report records reviews of around 100 customer relationships. It also records a third linked company whose review revealed potential money laundering concerns. Losses avoided are estimated, not observed.
The foreword's statement about neutralizing mule account networks is general and not tied to a documented outcome.

ai_role.statement: The HKMA report attributes the identification of Company C to the network analytics tool's matching of linked phone numbers and email addresses. A human relationship manager supplied the initial lead. Whether the tool uses machine learning is not stated. The bank built and deployed the tool itself. The HKMA, which wrote the report, is the regulator.

fields.account: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's report “AML/CFT Regtech: Case Studies and Insights” (January 2021; press release 21 January 2021) presents anonymized bank case studies. Bank F is a subsidiary and regional head office of a large global bank in Asia-Pacific, per the report. It implemented a network (graph) analytics solution in Hong Kong in 2013. It identified high-risk customers and transactions from wholesale client, correspondent banking, trade, payments and external registry data. In a 2015 example, a relationship manager gathered intelligence about trade-based money laundering (TBML) related to a drug cartel in one account. The manager linked it to a second account via the CRM tool. The tool then identified additional companies linked to the first two parties through linked phone numbers and email addresses. Account reviews for Companies A, B and C revealed potential money laundering concerns. The report states that by 2016 Bank F covered its top 20 commercial banking sites and about 80% of its trade lending book. The tool has led to review of around 100 customer relationships holding around USD 500 million in clean or unsecured exposures, it says. Even if 10% were unrecoverable, the tool contributed around USD 50 million in savings, it says. The foreword adds that such techniques are already neutralizing mule account networks linked to face mask scams. The 2015 example carries no day.
